04 / Two clues worth testing

Patterns that could explain lost capacity, but need a discriminating test.

RECHECK share by seal lot

Tester attempts, not unique products
SL-263.1% RECHECK
9,621 PASS · 308 RECHECK · 3 SCRAP · 9,932 attempts
SL-2730.8% RECHECK
2,368 PASS · 1,066 RECHECK · 22 SCRAP · 3,456 attempts
Signal: SL-27 has 10× the RECHECK share30.8% vs 3.1%. That could add tester load; it does not prove a material defect or explain the Oct 1 stop.

Completion-gap distributions before and after Sep 28

Compare completion-gap distributions before Sep 28 with the period from Sep 28 onward. The full shape matters: a longer right tail can signal more intermittent delays even when typical gaps barely move.

11,991 intervals · 6,309 before / 5,682 after
Before Sep 28Sep 28 onwardHover the plot for distribution details
ST20 · Before vs. after Sep 28
Median: 33.0s → 34.0s   ·   P90: 37.0s → 56.0s (+19.0s)
Means: 34.2s → 37.4s. Read the curves as descriptive evidence, not proof of a station-level cause.
Limitations: These are gaps between consecutive completion scans at a station, not unit processing durations. Gaps may include waiting, blocking, starvation, changeovers or missed scans. The split is descriptive, not a causal test; product mix, staffing and work orders are uncontrolled, and the synthetic observation window is short. A few extreme gaps can influence the tail. Confirm any signal against PLC states and buffer occupancy before attributing cause.

05 / What the support records add

The notes suggest extra tester workload; the material ledger shows a separate handoff gap. Neither record alone proves the cause of lost output.

The support notes raise a test-workload hypothesis

28 Sep · 17:31

Shift handover
Notes that the new SL-27 seal receipt is being used on some L assemblies and asks for clarity on how second checks should be classified.

29 Sep · 16:43

Engineering email · Kavya
Describes SL-27 as conditionally released and says RECHECK cycles are expected when the first trace is ambiguous; final disposition, not first run alone, should be used for shipment-quality assessment.

Interpretation: the documents support a credible mechanism for more tester activity and warn against treating every RECHECK as a confirmed defect. They do not quantify added cycle time or prove that retesting caused the B23 queue or output loss.

Picked is not delivered

Label ticket SD-1041, 1 Oct. The records show a handoff/posting gap—not proof that the line physically ran out at a specific second.

On Oct 1 E shift, ST40 has 52 minutes of HOLD in the shift KPI, while B34 briefly reaches capacity. Timing is consistent with a packing/label disruption; the ledger alone does not prove causality.

06 / What would settle it?

Connect buffer states, initiating events and tester disposition so the competing explanations can be separated.

Next-shift test

Three checks that separate competing explanations
1 / Record togetherOne-minute buffer counts + PLC states + manual interventions.
→
2 / Confirm initiating eventPhysical hold reason, label handover, alarm/trip timestamps.
→
3 / Compare matched shiftsTester occupancy and final dispositions for SL-26 vs SL-27.
Caveat: samples show minute-level states, not sub-minute order. MES scans record completions, not reliable station start times. RECHECK is not a confirmed defect. Repeated controller event IDs must be deduplicated.

07 / Buy evidence before buying a machine

Use a short, instrumented trial to distinguish tester workload from material-flow disruption before committing to equipment changes.

First intervention

A five-shift ST20 containment trial

Inspect/replace the torque bit, capture tip temperature and torque-confirmation retries, and log ST20 blocked time against B23 occupancy. Compare packed units and blocked minutes with matched shifts.

Success criteria: B23 spends less time at 9–10 units, ST20 blocked minutes fall, and packed output rises without shifting the queue to B34.

Parallel control

Close the line-side material loop

Require signed physical receipt for labels; separate request, pick, handover and posting timestamps. Track ST40 HOLD and B34 together during the trial.

Keep SL-27 first-pass RECHECK separate from confirmed scrap; review by lot and test attempt, not a single blended “quality” percentage.

Rejected for now · “The press is the root cause”

Press temperature warnings are real, and ST10 loss is high. But there is no corresponding controller trip, while the B23 queue and ST20 blocked time emerge together after Sep 28. Reconsider if synchronized press-trip records precede B23 growth and output loss.

Rejected for now · “SL-27 quality caused the whole dip”

SL-27 increases tester rechecks, but B23 changes on Sep 28 and persists across shifts; retest events alone don’t explain this buffer pattern. Reconsider if tester cycle-time/queue logs show retests consuming enough capacity to precede the throughput loss.

Limitations: synthetic short extract; shift-level KPIs are derivative; MES rows record stage completion, not starts; PLC event IDs include 78 duplicate resends; buffers are minute samples; material ledger lacks signed receipt; no synchronized torque trace or operator interview was supplied. These data identify a strong next test, not causal proof.
